newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia natural gas demand seen surging - economist.
newsitem.headline: Asia natural gas demand seen surging - economist.

text.p: Asia-Pacific demand for natural gas will likely surge as the region"s growing economies fuel energy demand, an economist said on Wednesday.

Natural gas demand in the Asia Pacific is expected to rise by an annual 5.3 percent until 2010 to reach 253.70 million tonnes LNG (liquefied natural gas) equivalent, Kazuya Fujime, managing director of the Institute of Energy Economics (IEE), told a symposium.
The countries covered in the study are; China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, South Korea, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei, Japan and Australia.

In 1993, natural gas accounted for a total 7.6 percent of primary energy demand in the countries covered in the study, excluding Australia, and is forecast to rise to around 10 percent by 2010, Fujime said.
Use of natural gas is low in Asian countries compared with global levels.
This is because countries in the region are not yet fully connected with natural gas pipelines, and because of the high cost of the infrastructure needed to trade LNG, Fujime said.
The largest consumer and importer of natural gas in Asia is Japan, which imported 39.40 million tonnes LNG equivalent in 1993, he said.
"Between 1993 and 2010, Japanese demand is is projected to grow by an annual three percent, much faster than the one percent growth estimated for primary energy demand," he said.
Taiwan and South Korea in particular are expected to sharply increase their LNG imports, reflecting growth in power generation, he said.
Taiwan"s LNG imports are seen growing an annual 13.3 percent between 1993 and 2010, while South Korean imports are seen increasing by an annual 9.3 percent over the same period, Fujime said.
He said Japan"s role in influencing the price formation would be undermined as other Asian countries expand their imports.

"Now that Korea and Taiwan are expanding their imports, and China and Thailand are taking part in the region"s gas markets, a growing number of players are involved in the price formation," Fujime said.
"As a result, ... , (the) pricing mechanism is expected to become more elastic and more intricate than ever," he said.
